body.en: This closing chapter puts the dot product (Chapter 1) to work: orthogonal bases make coordinates trivial to compute, the Gram–Schmidt process builds one out of any basis, and orthogonal projection turns "the line that best fits data with no exact solution" into a genuine, solvable system of equations — the least-squares method behind every linear regression.

Vectors \( \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \) are orthogonal if \( \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=0 \) (Chapter 1, Definition 1.2). A set \( \{\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k\} \) is an orthogonal set if every pair is orthogonal, and orthonormal if it's also orthogonal and every \( \lVert\mathbf{v}_i\rVert=1 \).

label.en: ▲ Theorem 8.1 — Orthogonal sets are linearly independent

body.en: If \( \{\mathbf{v}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{v}_k\} \) is an orthogonal set of nonzero vectors, it is linearly independent (Chapter 5, Definition 5.4).

Suppose \( c_1\mathbf{v}_1+c_2\mathbf{v}_2+\cdots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0} \). Dot both sides with \( \mathbf{v}_i \) for any fixed \( i \): \[ c_1(\mathbf{v}_1\cdot\mathbf{v}_i)+\cdots+c_i(\mathbf{v}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_i)+\cdots+c_k(\mathbf{v}_k\cdot\mathbf{v}_i)=0. \] Every term with \( j eq i \) vanishes since \( \mathbf{v}_j\cdot\mathbf{v}_i=0 \) (orthogonality), leaving just \( c_i(\mathbf{v}_i\cdot\mathbf{v}_i)=c_i\lVert\mathbf{v}_i Vert^2=0 \). Since \( \mathbf{v}_i eq\mathbf{0} \), \( \lVert\mathbf{v}_i Vert^2 eq0 \), forcing \( c_i=0 \). This holds for every \( i \), so the only solution is trivial: the set is linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of \( \mathbf{b} \) onto a nonzero vector \( \mathbf{a} \) is \[ \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b})=\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{a}. \] The residual \( \mathbf{b}-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b}) \) is always orthogonal to \( \mathbf{a} \): \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\big(\mathbf{b}-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b})\big)=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}-\frac{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a})=\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=0 \) — this decomposition of \( \mathbf{b} \) into a piece along \( \mathbf{a} \) plus a piece perpendicular to it is exactly what drives least squares below.

Turn the basis \( \mathbf{u}_1=(1,1,0) \), \( \mathbf{u}_2=(1,0,1) \) into an orthogonal one.

Keep \( \mathbf{w}_1=\mathbf{u}_1=(1,1,0) \). Subtract from \( \mathbf{u}_2 \) its projection onto \( \mathbf{w}_1 \), leaving only the part orthogonal to \( \mathbf{w}_1 \):

\[ \mathbf{w}_2=\mathbf{u}_2-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{w}_1}(\mathbf{u}_2)=(1,0,1)-\frac{1}{2}(1,1,0)=\left(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,1\right). \]

Check: \( \mathbf{w}_1\cdot\mathbf{w}_2=\tfrac12-\tfrac12+0=0 \). ✓ (Scaling \( \mathbf{w}_2 \) by 2 gives the tidier \( (1,-1,2) \), still orthogonal to \( \mathbf{w}_1 \).) With a third vector \( \mathbf{u}_3 \), the same idea repeats: subtract its projections onto both \( \mathbf{w}_1 \) and \( \mathbf{w}_2 \) to isolate the part orthogonal to both.

Given an inconsistent system \( A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} \) (more equations than the data actually satisfies exactly — the everyday case when fitting a line to noisy data), the least-squares solution \( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \) is the one minimizing \( \lVert A\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\mathbf{b}\rVert^2 \), the sum of squared residuals. \( A\hat{\mathbf{x}} \) turns out to be exactly the orthogonal projection of \( \mathbf{b} \) onto \( \operatorname{range}(A) \) (Chapter 7, Definition 7.2) — the closest point of that subspace to \( \mathbf{b} \), by the same perpendicular-residual idea as Definition 8.2 — and \( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \) solves the normal equations: \[ A^TA\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}=A^T\mathbf{b}. \]

Find the least-squares line \( y=mx+b \) through \( (1,1),(2,3),(3,4),(4,6) \).

Each point gives one equation \( mx_i+b=y_i \); in matrix form \( A\begin{pmatrix}m\\b\end{pmatrix}=\mathbf{y} \) with \( A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\2&1\\3&1\\4&1\end{pmatrix} \), \( \mathbf{y}=(1,3,4,6) \) — four equations, two unknowns, generally inconsistent.

\( A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}30&10\\10&4\end{pmatrix} \), \( A^T\mathbf{y}=\begin{pmatrix}43\\14\end{pmatrix} \). Solving \( A^TA\hat{\mathbf{x}}=A^T\mathbf{y} \): \( 30m+10b=43 \), \( 10m+4b=14 \). From the second, \( b=\frac{14-10m}{4} \); substituting: \( 30m+10\cdot\frac{14-10m}{4}=43\Rightarrow120m+140-100m=172\Rightarrow20m=32\Rightarrow m=1.6 \), then \( b=\frac{14-16}{4}=-0.5 \).

Least-squares line: \( y=1.6x-0.5 \).

value.en: Subtract projections onto earlier vectors, one at a time

body.en:
Find the orthogonal projection of \( \mathbf{b}=(4,3) \) onto \( \mathbf{a}=(1,2) \), and verify the residual is orthogonal to \( \mathbf{a} \).

Show solution

\( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=4+6=10 \), \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=1+4=5 \). \[ \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b})=\frac{10}{5}(1,2)=(2,4). \]

Residual \( =(4,3)-(2,4)=(2,-1) \). Check: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot(2,-1)=1(2)+2(-1)=2-2=0 \). Orthogonal, as guaranteed.

Is \( \left\{\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right),\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\right\} \) orthonormal?

Solution: Dot product: \( \tfrac12-\tfrac12=0 \) — orthogonal. Each has norm \( \sqrt{\tfrac12+\tfrac12}=1 \). Yes, orthonormal.

label.en: Distance from a point to a line via projection

body.en:
Find the distance from \( \mathbf{b}=(3,4) \) to the line through the origin spanned by \( \mathbf{a}=(1,0) \).

Solution: \( \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b})=\dfrac{3}{1}(1,0)=(3,0) \). Residual \( =(3,4)-(3,0)=(0,4) \).

Distance \( =\lVert(0,4)\rVert=4 \) — the perpendicular distance, exactly the residual's length.

solution.en: \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=10 \), \( \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{a}=4 \). \( \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{b})=\frac{10}{4}(2,0)=(5,0) \) — as expected, projecting onto the x-axis just keeps the x-coordinate.
